findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in SQLi page (low security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload 1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 records spanning the entire seeded users table: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — multiple distinct surnames disclosed via classic boolean-based UNION-less injection (OR tautology causes all rows to match). FALSE payload 1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records — page body contained only the 'User ID:' prompt with no ID/First name/Surname rows. This differential behavior (5 rows vs 0 rows) confirms unsanitized string concatenation of the 'id' parameter into the backend SQL query.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized 'ip' parameter in Ping utility (low security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Submitting ip=127.0.0.1; whoami caused the server to execute the chained shell command after the ping. Response body included the standard ping output (4 packets transmitted/received for 127.0.0.1) immediately followed by the literal string 'www-data' on its own line — the identity of the web server process user — proving the semicolon-separated 'whoami' command was executed server-side via unsanitized shell concatenation of the 'ip' field.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via unsanitized guestbook 'mtxMessage' field (low security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/  form_data={txtName: 'qa', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'}  (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After POSTing the canary payload (34 chars, within mtxMessage maxlength=50) with name 'qa', the guestbook page immediately echoed a new entry 'Name: qa Message:' with the script tag rendered unescaped in the HTML (visible as an empty message in the rendered text output since the script produces no visible text, consistent with raw HTML injection rather than encoding). On subsequent browser_navigate to the same page, browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the injected element's inner_text was 'window.xss_flag=1' — proving the stored <script> tag was parsed and executed by the browser on every page load, confirming persistent stored XSS.

findings.title: SQL Injection via POST id parameter (numeric boolean bypass) at medium security
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload TRUE: id=1 OR 1=1 returned 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith). Payload FALSE: id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (only the dropdown form, no 'First name/Surname' rows). This confirms the id field -- though rendered as a <select> dropdown in the HTML form -- is still vulnerable to numeric SQL injection via raw POST body manipulation, since quotes are escaped server-side at medium but numeric boolean injection bypasses the escaping. Footer confirmed 'Security Level: medium' on both responses.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass of ';' and '&&' blacklist at medium security
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload '127.0.0.1| whoami' bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which blocks ';' and '&&' substrings) by using a pipe character. Response pre_blocks contained exactly: 'www-data' -- the web server process identity -- confirming successful arbitrary command execution via the pipe operator. Footer confirmed 'Security Level: medium'.

findings.title: Stored XSS via mtxMessage field (maxlength bypass via raw POST) at medium security
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] The mtxMessage field has a client-side maxlength=50 HTML attribute (insufficient to block the 53-char canary), but since the payload was POSTed directly via raw form_data bypassing client-side length restriction, the full canary <script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script> was persisted unsanitized by the server (medium security only patches the txtName/reflected vectors, not mtxMessage). Upon reloading the guestbook page in an authenticated browser session, browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') located the injected live DOM element with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1', proving the injected <script> tag was rendered and executed by the browser rather than stripped.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (verified via browser_eval_js); element #test_token present in DOM with inner_html_excerpt 'window.xss_flag=1'

findings.title: SQL Injection via session-stored id (DVWA sqli, security=high)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # stored via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ rendered 5 records (bypassing the appended LIMIT 1 via trailing comment): ID: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith. FALSE control payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # rendered zero records (page showed only 'Click here to change your ID.' with no result rows). This TRUE(multiple rows)/FALSE(zero rows) differential confirms boolean-based SQL injection survives the high-security escaping and LIMIT-1 restriction via comment-out technique.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypassing high-security blacklist (DVWA exec, security=high)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist on ';', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&') produced response containing 'www-data' in the pre-formatted output block: pre_blocks: ["www-data"], visible_text snippet: 'Enter an IP address: www-data'. Footer confirmed Security Level: high. This proves command injection yields the web-server process identity (www-data), satisfying the confirmation criterion.

findings.title: Stored XSS via guestbook message (DVWA xss_s, security=high)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Canary payload <script id="x">window.xss_flag=1</script> (49 chars, within mtxMessage maxlength=50) was submitted as the guestbook message and persisted (visible in subsequent page loads as entry 'Name: tester2'). After navigating to the guestbook page in an authenticated browser context, browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned 1, proving the injected inline script executed in the victim's browser context despite high-security level, confirming stored XSS.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (evaluated result: 1) after browser_navigate to http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ as dvwa_admin following stored payload submission.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket by ID
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1, Bearer=acct1 token) -> 200, basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3]

GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct2, Bearer=acct2 token, own_basket_id=7) -> 200, basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3] -- IDENTICAL to acct1's own basket despite acct2 using its own token
findings.response_evidence: acct1 (own_basket_id=6) GET /rest/basket/6 returned: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}]}}. acct2 (own_basket_id=7, a distinct different basket belonging to UserId=23) was then used to GET /rest/basket/6 (NOT its own basket id=7) and received HTTP 200 with the exact same data: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}]}}. No 403/401 authorization check was enforced - acct2's Bearer token successfully retrieved acct1's distinct seeded basket contents (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty 3), confirming a Broken Object Level Authorization vulnerability.

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass via SQL Injection in email field
findings.response_evidence: Response HTTP 200: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected payload email=\"' OR 1=1--\" closed the SQL string literal and appended an always-true condition, bypassing password verification entirely and causing the backend query (likely `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='<input>' AND password='[REDACTED]'`) to match the first user record in the table. The response confirms a valid authentication JWT was issued for umail=\"admin@juice-sh.op\" (the first/admin user) and bid (basket id)=1, without ever supplying the correct admin password - a clear authentication bypass via SQL injection.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection via unsanitized q parameter
findings.response_evidence: 1) Single-quote payload q=qwert' returned HTTP 500 with body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" - proving the q parameter is concatenated directly into a raw SQL query without parameterization/escaping, causing a backend SQL syntax error. 2) The crafted UNION payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- closed the malformed WHERE clause and injected a 9-column UNION SELECT matching the products table's column count, returning HTTP 200 with a benign fabricated product record: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} - demonstrating successful arbitrary SQL injection/UNION-based data retrieval capability.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index directory listing (visible_text): 'listing directory /ftp/ ... acquisitions.md 909 ... package.json.bak 4291 ...' confirming acquisitions.md is openly listed among other sensitive files (incident-support.kdbx, coupons_2013.md.bak, suspicious_errors.yml) without authentication.
2) GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ...' confirming the confidential acquisition memo is directly retrievable by an unauthenticated user via the open directory listing.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal Bypasses File-Extension Allowlist on /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' and stack trace referencing 'at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)', confirming the extension-allowlist middleware blocks the raw .bak file.
2) GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with body containing the full restricted package.json content: '{\n  \"name\": \"juice-shop\",\n  \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", ... \"dependencies\": {...} ...}'. This proves the null-byte suffix satisfies the .md extension check while the underlying filesystem read still serves package.json.bak, confirming the path traversal / filter bypass.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access to /api/Feedbacks Discloses User PII (Email Fragments + UserId Linkage)
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /api/Feedbacks returned HTTP 200 with a JSON array of 8 feedback records fully readable without any auth token. Records disclose: (a) numeric UserId foreign keys linking feedback to specific registered accounts (UserId 1, 2, 3, 21), and (b) author email-address fragments embedded directly in the comment text revealing domain and partial local-part, e.g. comment id=1 'I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)', id=2 '(***@juice-sh.op)', id=3 '(***der@juice-sh.op)', id=4 '... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)' alongside a leaked wallet seed phrase 'purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch'. This endpoint requires no authentication yet exposes personally-identifiable linkage (UserId + partial email) for arbitrary users, confirming unauthenticated PII exposure.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory with Browsable Listing and Sensitive Key File Disclosure
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ (Accept: text/html,application/json) -> HTTP 200, serve-index directory listing
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with content_type text/html and a rendered directory listing page titled 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/' containing visible_text: 'Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM' and hyperlinks to both files, confirming the directory is browsable (serve-index) and unauthenticated.
2) GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key returned HTTP 200 (content_type application/octet-stream) with body: '1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42' — a sensitive premium-feature unlock key.
3) GET /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub returned HTTP 200 (content_type application/x-mspublisher) with body: '-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----\nMIGJAoGBAM3CosR73CBNcJsLv5E90NsFt6qN1uziQ484gbOoule8leXHFbyIzPQRozgEpSpiwhr6d2/c0CfZHEJ3m5tV0klxfjfM7oqjRMURnH/rmBjcETQ7qzIISZQ/iptJ3p7Gi78X5ZMhLNtDkUFU9WaGdiEb+SnC39wjErmJSfmGb7i1AgMBAAE=\n-----END RSA PUBLIC KEY-----' — the application's JWT verification public key.
Both the directory listing and the direct retrieval of the two sensitive key files succeeded without authentication, confirming CWE-548 Exposed Encryption Keys Directory.
